MANILA, Philippines – Rosal (Champi) weakened from a super typhoon into a typhoon on Thursday afternoon, October 22, but rainfall and wind warnings have yet to be lifted for portions of Northern Luzon.

The Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical, and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) said in its 5 pm bulletin on Thursday that Rosal’s maximum sustained winds are down to 165 kilometers per hour. Its gustiness has also eased to 205 km/h.
At its peak, Rosal had maximum sustained winds of 215 km/h.

As of 4 pm on Thursday, the typhoon was located 350 kilometers east of Itbayat, Batanes, moving northwest at only 15 km/h. It will be at its closest point to extreme Northern Luzon between Thursday afternoon and Friday morning, October 23.
PAGASA said Rosal will continue to trigger heavy to intense rain in Batanes (100-200 millimeters) and moderate to heavy rain in Cagayan (50-100 mm) in the next 24 hours.

On Thursday evening, the typhoon may also bring rain with gusty winds to Ilocos Norte, Apayao, and Isabela, as well as scattered rain and thunderstorms to the rest of the Cordillera Administrative Region, the rest of Cagayan Valley, Ilocos Sur, La Union, and Aurora.

The weather bureau added that Rosal’s trough or extension might cause scattered rain and thunderstorms in Bicol, the Zamboanga Peninsula, Western Visayas, the Negros Island Region, Lanao del Norte, Misamis Occidental, and Palawan.

blocks.text: Rosal is still projected to leave the Philippine Area of Responsibility by Friday evening or early Saturday morning, October 24. It entered PAR on Tuesday, October 20.
After leaving PAR, Rosal is likely to be downgraded to a severe tropical storm on Saturday.
Rosal is the Philippines’ 18th tropical cyclone for 2026, and the first for October. PAGASA earlier estimated the country may have one or two tropical cyclones during the month.
The Philippines is currently in a transition period to the northeast monsoon or amihan, following the end of the southwest monsoon or habagat, which was announced last October 5.

The northeast monsoon typically brings surges of cold temperatures, but the upcoming amihan period could be warmer as the existing strong El Niño in the tropical Pacific Ocean is predicted to become very strong in the fourth quarter of 2026. – Rappler.com
